\section{Introduction}

\subsection{The objects}

Fix a preorder $A$ (the \emph{clock}) and a set $B$ (the \emph{switches}). A \textbf{clock-and-switch world} over $(A,B)$ is a pair
\[
  w = (\mathrm{clock}(w),\ \mathrm{switch}(w)) \in A \times (B \to \{\onn,\off\}),
\]
ordered by
\[
  w \le v \quad :\Longleftrightarrow\quad \mathrm{clock}(w) \le \mathrm{clock}(v)
  \ \text{ and }\ \forall b \in B,\ \bigl(\mathrm{switch}(w)_b = \onn \Rightarrow \mathrm{switch}(v)_b = \onn\bigr).
\]
Write $\CW(A,B)$ for the resulting preorder and $\CW(n,m) := \CW([n],[m])$, where $[n] = \{0 < 1 < \dots < n-1\}$. This is the canonical model of \emph{monotone resource accumulation}: time advances, commitments are made and never unmade.

\begin{proposition}\label{prop:basic}
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*)]
  \item If $A$ is a partial order then so is $\CW(A,B)$; in particular $\CW(n,m)$ is a finite partial order with $n \cdot 2^m$ elements.
  \item If $A$ has a least element then $\CW(A,B)$ is rooted, with root ``clock at the bottom, all switches off''.
  \item If $A$ is a join-semilattice then $\CW(A,B)$ is directed:
  $w, v \le (\mathrm{clock}(w) \vee \mathrm{clock}(v),\ \mathrm{switch}(w) \cup \mathrm{switch}(v))$.
\end{enumerate}
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
(i) If $w \le v \le w$, the clocks agree by antisymmetry in $A$, and a switch on in one is on in the other in both directions, so the configurations agree pointwise. (ii), (iii) are the displayed witnesses. The cardinality claim is the order isomorphism $\CW(A,B) \cong A \times (B \to \{0,1\})$ onto the product order.
\end{proof}

\subsection{Faithful quotients}

\begin{definition}
Let $X, Y$ be preorders. A map $f : X \to Y$ is a \textbf{bounded morphism} (p-morphism) if
\begin{itemize}
  \item \textbf{(Forth)} $x \le y \Rightarrow f(x) \le f(y)$, and
  \item \textbf{(Back)} $f(x) \le q \Rightarrow \exists\, y \ge x$ with $f(y) = q$.
\end{itemize}
\end{definition}

Bounded morphisms compose. The back condition prevents the map from inventing or destroying local possibility: the future of $f(x)$ in $Y$ is exactly the $f$-image of the future of $x$ in $X$. Logically, a surjective bounded morphism preserves and reflects the validity of every modal formula.

\begin{definition}
A preorder $P$ is \textbf{representable} if there are $n,m \in \mathbb{N}$ and a surjective bounded morphism $\CW(n,m) \twoheadrightarrow P$.
\end{definition}

\begin{example}[Forget the switches]\label{ex:forget}
$w \mapsto \mathrm{clock}(w)$ is a surjective bounded morphism $\CW(A,B) \twoheadrightarrow A$. Back: to realise $a \ge \mathrm{clock}(w)$, move to $(a, \mathrm{switch}(w))$.
\end{example}

\begin{example}[Count the switches]\label{ex:count}
$w \mapsto \#\{b : \mathrm{switch}(w)_b = \onn\}$ is a surjective bounded morphism $\CW(1,m) \twoheadrightarrow [m+1]$. Back: to raise the count, turn on more switches.
\end{example}

\subsection{Terminology}

Throughout, $P$ is a finite preorder. It is \emph{rooted} if some $r$ satisfies $r \le p$ for all $p$; \emph{directed} if any two points have a common upper bound; \emph{antisymmetric} (a poset) if $p \le q \le p$ implies $p=q$. The \emph{cluster} of $p_0$ is $C(p_0) = \{p : p \le p_0 \text{ and } p_0 \le p\}$; clusters partition $P$ and are singletons exactly when $P$ is a poset. The \emph{antisymmetrisation} $P/\!\!\approx$ is the poset of clusters. The \emph{height} of $P$ is the largest $\ell$ with a strictly increasing chain $c_0 < \dots < c_\ell$ (meaning $c_i \le c_{i+1}$, $c_{i+1} \not\le c_i$).

\begin{lemma}\label{lem:top}
A finite nonempty directed preorder has a greatest element.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
By induction on finite subsets: the empty set has an arbitrary upper bound, and given an upper bound $z$ of $S$ and a new point $a$, directedness supplies an upper bound of $\{a,z\}$, which bounds $S \cup \{a\}$. Apply to the whole carrier.
\end{proof}

\section{The representation theorem}

\subsection{The greedy climb}

\begin{definition}
A \textbf{linear extension enumeration} of a finite nonempty poset $P$ with $k = |P|$ is a listing $t_0,\dots,t_{k-1}$ of all points such that $t_i \le t_j \Rightarrow i \le j$. Such an enumeration always exists.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Greedy climb]\label{def:climb}
Let $P$ be a finite poset with root $r$, top $\top$ and linear extension enumeration $t$. For $s : \mathbb{N} \to \{\onn,\off\}$ set
\[
  W_s(0) = r, \qquad
  W_s(i+1) =
  \begin{cases}
    t_i & \text{if } s_i = \onn \text{ and } W_s(i) \le t_i,\\
    \top & \text{if } s_i = \onn \text{ and } W_s(i) \not\le t_i,\\
    W_s(i) & \text{if } s_i = \off .
  \end{cases}
\]
The \textbf{greedy climb map} is $\Phi(w) = W_{\mathrm{switch}(w)}(k)$ on $\CW(1,k)$.
\end{definition}

Note that $W_s(i)$ depends only on $s_0,\dots,s_{i-1}$, and that the all-off configuration stays at $r$.

\begin{lemma}[Forth]\label{lem:forth}
If $s_l = \onn \Rightarrow s'_l = \onn$ for all $l$, then $W_s(i) \le W_{s'}(i)$ for all $i$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Induction on $i$. Suppose $W_s(i) \le W_{s'}(i)$. If $s_i = \off$ then $W_s(i+1) = W_s(i) \le W_{s'}(i) \le W_{s'}(i+1)$, since a single step never descends. If $s_i = \onn$ then $s'_i = \onn$; if $W_{s'}(i) \le t_i$ then $W_s(i) \le t_i$ as well and both sides step to $t_i$; otherwise the right-hand side steps to $\top$, which dominates everything.
\end{proof}

\begin{example}[Failure of the naive climb]\label{ex:diamond}
Let $P$ be the diamond $0 < a,b < 1$ with $a,b$ incomparable, enumerated $0,a,b,1$. Under the naive rule (stand still instead of jumping to $\top$), configuration $\{b\}$ climbs to $b$ while the larger configuration $\{a,b\}$ climbs to $a$; since $b \not\le a$, monotonicity fails. The ``jump to the top'' clause repairs exactly this.
\end{example}

\begin{lemma}[Back]\label{lem:back}
Let $t$ be a linear extension enumeration, $k' \le k$, and let $s$ satisfy $W_s(k') \le t_j$ with $j < k'$. Then there is $s' \supseteq s$ (on-sets only grow) with $W_{s'}(k') = t_j$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
Induction on the number of steps. The linear extension property is the essential point: every point below $t_j$ occurs at an index $\le j$, so turning on switch $j$ and leaving earlier switches as they are leaves the climb below $t_j$ on arrival at index $j$; the ``$\le t_i$'' branch fires and the climb lands on $t_j$, and no later switch moves it away.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Representation]\label{thm:rep}
Every finite rooted directed partial order $P$ is a surjective bounded morphic image of $\CW(1,|P|)$, via the greedy climb along any linear extension enumeration.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Let $r$ be the root and $\top$ the top (Lemma~\ref{lem:top}). Forth is Lemma~\ref{lem:forth}; Back is Lemma~\ref{lem:back}, whose output configuration has all the switches of $w$ still on, hence gives a world $\ge w$. Surjectivity is Back applied at the all-off world, whose image is $r \le t_j$ for every $j$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Sharp switch count, upper bound]\label{thm:sharpup}
Every finite rooted directed poset $P$ is a surjective bounded morphic image of $\CW(1, |P|-1)$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
In a linear extension of a rooted poset, $t_0 = r$, and the switch attached to the root is a no-op. Re-index so switch $i$ carries $t_{i+1}$; the back condition acquires one extra case, namely that the root is reached with no switches on, which uses antisymmetry.
\end{proof}

Moreover, forgetting the last $b$ switches is a surjective bounded morphism $\CW(1,a+b) \twoheadrightarrow \CW(1,a)$: spare switches are harmless.

\subsection{The obstruction}

\begin{theorem}[Antisymmetry is inherited]\label{thm:antisymm}
Let $X$ be a finite partial order, $Y$ a preorder, and $f : X \twoheadrightarrow Y$ a surjective bounded morphism. Then $Y$ is antisymmetric.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Let $p \le q$ and $q \le p$ in $Y$, and write $p = f(x_0)$. Put $S = \{x \in X : f(x) = p \text{ or } f(x) = q\}$, a nonempty finite subset of a finite poset, and choose $x \in S$ maximal; thus $y \in S$ and $x \le y$ imply $y = x$.

If $f(x) = p$, then from $p \le q$ Back gives $y \ge x$ with $f(y) = q$, so $y \in S$, $y = x$, and $p = q$. If $f(x) = q$, then from $q \le p$ Back gives $y \ge x$ with $f(y) = p$, so again $y = x$ and $p = q$.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}\label{cor:cluster}
Let $K$ be the two-element preorder in which both points are below each other. Then $K$ is finite, rooted and directed, but is not a bounded morphic image of any $\CW(n,m)$.
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
$\CW(n,m)$ is a finite poset by Proposition~\ref{prop:basic}(i), so Theorem~\ref{thm:antisymm} would force $K$ antisymmetric.
\end{proof}

Hence the literal filtration statement ``every finite rooted directed preorder is a bounded morphic image of some $\CW(n,m)$'' is false, with a two-point counterexample.

\subsection{The characterisation}

\begin{theorem}[Characterisation]\label{thm:char}
A finite nonempty preorder $P$ is representable if and only if it is rooted, directed and antisymmetric.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
($\Rightarrow$) A surjection forces $n \ge 1$; rootedness and directedness are pushed forward through Forth, and antisymmetry is Theorem~\ref{thm:antisymm}. ($\Leftarrow$) Antisymmetry upgrades $P$ to a poset, and Theorem~\ref{thm:rep} (or Theorem~\ref{thm:sharpup}) applies with $n = 1$.
\end{proof}

\section{Closure properties}

All orders below are finite and nonempty.

\begin{theorem}\label{thm:closure}
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*)]
  \item If $P \cong Q$ and $P$ is representable, so is $Q$.
  \item If $P$ and $Q$ are representable, so is $P \times Q$; more generally $\prod_{i \in \iota} P_i$ is representable for a finite index set $\iota$ and representable factors.
  \item If $P$ is representable and $p \in P$, the principal filter $\uparrow\!p = \{q : p \le q\}$ is representable.
  \item Every finite lattice with least and greatest elements is representable; in particular every finite Boolean algebra and every finite chain.
  \item Representability passes to surjective bounded morphic images.
\end{enumerate}
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
By Theorem~\ref{thm:char} it suffices to verify rootedness, directedness and antisymmetry in each case. (i) Transport along the isomorphism. (ii) Coordinatewise: root $(r_P,r_Q)$, coordinatewise upper bounds, coordinatewise antisymmetry. (iii) $\uparrow\!p$ is rooted at $p$; if $x,y \ge p$ have common upper bound $z$ in $P$, then $p \le x \le z$, so $z \in \uparrow\!p$; antisymmetry is inherited by subsets. (iv) Root $\bot$, directedness by $x \vee y$, antisymmetry by definition of a lattice order. (v) Compose the morphisms.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}
The dual of (iii) fails: a principal ideal $\downarrow\!p$ need not be directed.
\end{remark}

\section{Resource bounds}

\subsection{The rank grading}

\begin{definition}
The \textbf{rank} of $w \in \CW(n,m)$ is $\rk(w) = \mathrm{clock}(w) + \#\{b : \mathrm{switch}(w)_b = \onn\} \in \{0,\dots,n+m-1\}$.
\end{definition}

\begin{lemma}\label{lem:rank}
$\rk$ is monotone, and strictly monotone: $w \le v$, $w \ne v$ imply $\rk(w) < \rk(v)$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Both summands are monotone. If the ranks are equal, the clocks are equal (the clock cannot decrease), and the on-sets have equal size while one contains the other, so they coincide; thus $w = v$.
\end{proof}

\begin{proposition}[Cardinality bound]\label{prop:card}
If $\CW(n,m) \twoheadrightarrow P$ then $|P| \le n \cdot 2^m$.
\end{proposition}

\begin{theorem}[Chain lifting]\label{thm:lift}
Let $f : \CW(n,m) \twoheadrightarrow P$ be a surjective bounded morphism and $c_0,\dots,c_\ell$ a strictly increasing chain in $P$. Then some $w$ has $\rk(w) \ge \ell$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Induct on $\ell$. Given $w_i$ with $f(w_i) = c_i$ and $\rk(w_i) \ge i$, apply Back to $c_i \le c_{i+1}$ to get $w_{i+1} \ge w_i$ with $f(w_{i+1}) = c_{i+1}$. Since $c_{i+1} \not\le c_i$ we have $w_{i+1} \ne w_i$, so $\rk(w_{i+1}) > \rk(w_i) \ge i$ by Lemma~\ref{lem:rank}. No dependent choice is needed: the chain is lifted inside a single induction.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Height bound]\label{cor:height}
If $P$ is a surjective bounded morphic image of $\CW(n,m)$ and contains a strictly increasing chain with $\ell+1$ points, then $\ell < n+m$; equivalently $\hgt(P) \le n+m-1$.
\end{corollary}

The two bounds are independent: the cardinality bound is logarithmic in $|P|$ and blind to shape, the height bound linear in chain length and blind to width.

\subsection{Chains, and the roles of the two resources}

\begin{theorem}[Exact switch count for chains]\label{thm:chaincount}
For all $\ell,m \ge 0$, there is a surjective bounded morphism $\CW(1,m) \twoheadrightarrow [\ell+1]$ if and only if $\ell \le m$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
($\Rightarrow$) Corollary~\ref{cor:height} with $n=1$. ($\Leftarrow$) Theorem~\ref{thm:sharpup} supplies a morphism from $\CW(1,\ell)$; extra switches are harmless.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}
The least $m$ with $\CW(1,m) \twoheadrightarrow [\ell+1]$ is exactly $\ell$, attained by the switch-counting morphism of Example~\ref{ex:count}. That example is therefore optimal, not merely illustrative.
\end{corollary}

\begin{theorem}[Switchless worlds are exactly the chains]\label{thm:switchless}
A finite nonempty preorder is a surjective bounded morphic image of some $\CW(n,0)$ if and only if it is a linear order.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
($\Rightarrow$) $\CW(n,0)$ is totally ordered, and Forth pushes totality forward; antisymmetry is Theorem~\ref{thm:antisymm}. ($\Leftarrow$) A finite linear order with $k$ elements is isomorphic to $\CW(k,0)$, and order isomorphisms are bounded morphisms.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[The clock is redundant]\label{thm:clockred}
A finite nonempty preorder is representable if and only if it is a surjective bounded morphic image of a one-tick world $\CW(1,m)$ for some $m$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Representability gives rootedness, directedness and antisymmetry (Theorem~\ref{thm:char}); Theorem~\ref{thm:rep} then gives a one-tick representation. The converse is trivial.
\end{proof}

Thus switches subsume clocks, while clocks cannot subsume switches: all branching in a representable order is paid for in switches.

\subsection{Modal transfer}

Read a preorder $X$ as a Kripke frame with accessibility $\le$, and write $X \models \varphi$ for validity of a modal formula.

\begin{theorem}[p-morphism lemma]\label{thm:pmorph}
If $f : X \to Y$ is a bounded morphism of preorders, $V$ a valuation on $Y$ and $\varphi$ a modal formula, then $x \Vdash_{V \circ f} \varphi$ iff $f(x) \Vdash_V \varphi$. Consequently, if $f$ is surjective then $X \models \varphi$ implies $Y \models \varphi$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Induction on $\varphi$; only $\Box\psi$ is nontrivial, where Forth gives one implication and Back the other.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Modal theory of clock-and-switch worlds]\label{thm:modal}
A modal formula is valid on every finite rooted directed poset if and only if it is valid on every $\CW(n,m)$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Every nonempty $\CW(n,m)$ is itself a finite rooted directed poset (the case $n=0$ being vacuous), which gives one direction. Conversely, Theorem~\ref{thm:rep} and Theorem~\ref{thm:pmorph} transfer validity from $\CW(1,|P|)$ to any finite rooted directed poset $P$.
\end{proof}

\begin{example}[S4.2 by transfer]
The axiom $\Diamond\Box p \to \Box\Diamond p$ is valid on any directed preorder: if some $u \ge x$ forces $\Box p$ and $y \ge x$, directedness gives $z \ge u,y$ with $z \Vdash p$, so $y \Vdash \Diamond p$. Verifying this on $\CW(n,m)$ uses only the explicit directedness of Proposition~\ref{prop:basic}(iii); Theorem~\ref{thm:modal} then exports it to every finite rooted directed poset.
\end{example}

\section{Phase-augmented worlds}

\subsection{Why the obvious repairs fail}

Theorem~\ref{thm:antisymm} uses only two properties of the source: finiteness and antisymmetry. Hence enlarging the source class by a product with an \emph{ordered} factor changes nothing (the product is again a finite poset), and quotienting a poset by an order-compatible equivalence changes nothing (such a quotient is again a poset). Clusters must be produced by multiplying with a factor the order cannot see.

\subsection{The definition}

\begin{definition}[Phase-augmented world]
For $c \ge 0$, a \textbf{phase-augmented clock-and-switch world} is a pair $w = (\mathrm{base}(w), \mathrm{phase}(w)) \in \CW(A,B) \times [c]$ ordered by
\[
  w \le v \quad :\Longleftrightarrow\quad \mathrm{base}(w) \le \mathrm{base}(v).
\]
Write $\CW_c(A,B)$, and $\CW_c(n,m)$ in the finite case. Equivalently, $\CW_c(A,B)$ is the product of $\CW(A,B)$ with the $c$-element \emph{indiscrete} preorder.
\end{definition}

\begin{proposition}\label{prop:phasebasic}
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*)]
  \item $|\CW_c(n,m)| = n \cdot 2^m \cdot c$.
  \item $\CW_c(A,B)$ is rooted when $A$ has a least element and $c \ge 1$, and directed when $A$ is a join-semilattice.
  \item If $c \ge 2$ and $A \ne \emptyset$, $\CW_c(A,B)$ is not antisymmetric: any two states with the same base and different phases form a two-element cluster.
  \item Forgetting the phase, $w \mapsto \mathrm{base}(w)$, is a surjective bounded morphism $\CW_c(A,B) \twoheadrightarrow \CW(A,B)$ for $c \ge 1$.
\end{enumerate}
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
(i) is the product bijection; (ii) copies Proposition~\ref{prop:basic} with any phase attached; (iii) is the displayed pair; (iv) Forth is the definition and Back is trivial --- to realise $u \ge \mathrm{base}(w)$, move to $(u,\mathrm{phase}(w))$.
\end{proof}

Item (iv) is the third structural projection of the theory, alongside Examples~\ref{ex:forget} and~\ref{ex:count}.

\begin{definition}
$P$ is \textbf{phase-representable} if there are $n,m,c$ and a surjective bounded morphism $\CW_c(n,m) \twoheadrightarrow P$.
\end{definition}

Every representable preorder is phase-representable: compose with the forget-the-phase morphism at $c=1$.

\subsection{The filtration lemma for preorders}

\begin{theorem}[Filtration lemma, sharp form]\label{thm:filtration}
Let $P$ be a finite nonempty rooted directed preorder in which every cluster has at most $c$ elements, and let $m = |P/\!\!\approx|$ be the number of clusters. Then $P$ is a surjective bounded morphic image of $\CW_c(1,m)$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Let $Q = P/\!\!\approx$, $\pi : P \to Q$ the quotient and $\rho : Q \to P$ a section with $\pi\rho = \mathrm{id}$. The defining property of the antisymmetrisation is
\[
  \pi(a) \le \pi(b) \iff a \le b .
\]
Hence $Q$ is a finite nonempty rooted directed \emph{poset}, and Theorem~\ref{thm:rep} supplies a surjective bounded morphism $f : \CW(1,|Q|) \twoheadrightarrow Q$.

The fibres of $\pi$ are exactly the clusters, so each has at most $c$ elements; fix injections $e_q : \pi^{-1}(q) \hookrightarrow [c]$ and define
\[
  \pick(q,j) =
  \begin{cases}
    \text{the unique } p \in \pi^{-1}(q) \text{ with } e_q(p) = j, & \text{if it exists},\\
    \rho(q), & \text{otherwise}.
  \end{cases}
\]
Then $\pi(\pick(q,j)) = q$ always, and for every $p$ there is $j$ with $\pick(\pi(p),j) = p$, namely $j = e_{\pi(p)}(p)$ (\emph{fibre-surjectivity}).

Set $F(w) = \pick\bigl(f(\mathrm{base}(w)), \mathrm{phase}(w)\bigr)$.

\emph{Forth.} $w \le v$ gives $f(\mathrm{base}(w)) \le f(\mathrm{base}(v))$, i.e.\ $\pi(F(w)) \le \pi(F(v))$, i.e.\ $F(w) \le F(v)$.

\emph{Back.} If $F(w) \le p$ then $f(\mathrm{base}(w)) = \pi(F(w)) \le \pi(p)$, so Back for $f$ gives $u \ge \mathrm{base}(w)$ with $f(u) = \pi(p)$; choosing $j$ with $\pick(\pi(p),j) = p$ yields $(u,j) \ge w$ and $F(u,j) = p$.

\emph{Surjectivity.} Pick $w_0$ with $f(w_0) = \pi(p)$ and $j$ with $\pick(\pi(p),j)=p$; then $F(w_0,j) = p$.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[The mission statement, repaired]\label{cor:mission}
Every finite nonempty rooted directed preorder --- no antisymmetry assumed --- is a surjective bounded morphic image of some $\CW_c(n,m)$.
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
Apply Theorem~\ref{thm:filtration} with $c = |P|$.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}
The two-element cluster of Corollary~\ref{cor:cluster} is phase-representable, with two phases.
\end{corollary}

\subsection{The converse: phases are metered by cluster size}

\begin{theorem}[Cluster bound]\label{thm:clusterbound}
If $f : \CW_c(n,m) \twoheadrightarrow P$ is a surjective bounded morphism, then every cluster of $P$ has at most $c$ elements.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Fix $p_0$ and let $C = C(p_0)$. Consider the set of bases of preimages of $C$,
\[
  S = \{u \in \CW(n,m) : \exists j \in [c],\ f(u,j) \in C\},
\]
which is nonempty and finite; since $\CW(n,m)$ is a partial order, choose $u \in S$ maximal.

Let $p \in C$ and let $j_0$ witness $u \in S$. Since $C$ is a cluster, $f(u,j_0) \le p_0 \le p$, so Back gives $y = (y_b,y_p) \ge (u,j_0)$ with $f(y) = p$. Then $y_b \ge u$ and $y_b \in S$, so maximality forces $y_b = u$, whence $f(u,y_p) = p$. Therefore $C \subseteq \{f(u,j) : j \in [c]\}$, a set of at most $c$ elements.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Characterisation of phase-representability]\label{thm:charC}
A finite nonempty preorder is phase-representable if and only if it is rooted and directed.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
($\Rightarrow$) A surjection forces $n, c \ge 1$, and rootedness and directedness are inherited from $\CW_c(n,m)$ through Forth. ($\Leftarrow$) Corollary~\ref{cor:mission}.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Sharpness of the phase count]\label{thm:sharpphase}
Let $P$ be a finite nonempty rooted directed preorder and $c \ge 0$. Then there is $m$ with $\CW_c(1,m) \twoheadrightarrow P$ if and only if every cluster of $P$ has at most $c$ elements. Consequently the least admissible number of phases equals the maximal cluster size of $P$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Combine Theorems~\ref{thm:clusterbound} and~\ref{thm:filtration}.
\end{proof}

Compared with Theorem~\ref{thm:char}, the antisymmetry clause has disappeared. It has not been ignored but bought, at a price recorded exactly by Theorem~\ref{thm:sharpphase}.

\section{Algorithms}

\begin{algorithmx}[Greedy climb representation]
\emph{Input:} a finite rooted directed poset $P$. \emph{Output:} the map $\Phi : \CW(1,|P|) \to P$.
\begin{enumerate}
  \item Compute the root $r$ and the top $\top$.
  \item Compute a linear extension $t_0,\dots,t_{k-1}$ by topological sort.
  \item For each of the $2^k$ switch configurations $s$: set $w \leftarrow r$; for $i = 0,\dots,k-1$, if $s_i$ is on, set $w \leftarrow t_i$ when $w \le t_i$ and $w \leftarrow \top$ otherwise. Emit $\Phi(s) = w$.
\end{enumerate}
Tabulating the whole map costs $O(2^k k)$ comparisons; each individual image costs $O(k)$.
\end{algorithmx}

\begin{algorithmx}[Minimal switch number by pruned search]
For increasing $m$, enumerate candidate maps $\CW(1,m) \to P$ by assigning values to cube vertices in order of increasing popcount, pruning as soon as monotonicity fails against an assigned predecessor; test Back and surjectivity at each complete assignment. The outer loop is pruned by $2^m \ge |P|$ and $m \ge \hgt(P)$.
\end{algorithmx}

\begin{algorithmx}[Phase-augmented representation]
\emph{Input:} a finite rooted directed preorder $P$. \emph{Output:} a surjective bounded morphism $\CW_c(1,m) \twoheadrightarrow P$ with $c$ the maximal cluster size and $m$ the number of clusters.
\begin{enumerate}
  \item Compute clusters by mutual accessibility; set $c = \max_i |C_i|$ and $m$ their number.
  \item Build the antisymmetrisation $Q$ and check it is a rooted directed poset.
  \item Run the greedy climb on $Q$ to obtain $f$.
  \item Fix a fibre-surjective $\pick$, e.g.\ $\pick(i,j) = p_{i,\min(j,|C_i|-1)}$ for an enumeration $C_i = \{p_{i,0},\dots\}$.
  \item Emit $F(w,j) = \pick(f(w),j)$.
\end{enumerate}
Cluster computation is $O(|P|^2)$; step 3 dominates at $O(2^m m)$.
\end{algorithmx}

\section{Discussion}

The characterisation says that the finite state spaces expressible by a monotone-resource machine, up to possibility-preserving quotient, are exactly those with a definite initial state, no permanently divergent branches, and no observationally indistinguishable duplicates. The first two are structural facts about the process; the third is observational, and the phase-augmented theory identifies precisely what must be added to the machine to allow it: hidden state, in the exact quantity of the indistinguishability it must support.

The resource bounds read cleanly: width is paid for logarithmically in switches, height linearly in ticks-plus-switches, and indistinguishability linearly in phases, at exactly one phase per indistinguishable alternative. Theorem~\ref{thm:modal} turns a semantic question about an unwieldy class of frames into a question about a single structured family.

Some questions are left open. Theorem~\ref{thm:sharpup} gives $|P|-1$ switches, matched by the height bound only on chains; the exact switch number of a general poset is not determined here. Likewise Theorem~\ref{thm:filtration} uses one switch per cluster, which is not claimed optimal.

\section{Future directions}

\begin{conjecture}[Switch number as an order invariant]
Define $\mathrm{sw}(P)$ to be the least $m$ with a surjective bounded morphism $\CW(1,m) \twoheadrightarrow P$. Then $\mathrm{sw}$ is not determined by $(|P|,\hgt(P))$, but is determined by the cover-branching profile
\[
  \mathrm{sw}(P) = \max_{C \text{ maximal chain}} \bigl(|C| - 1 + b(C)\bigr),
\]
where $b(C)$ counts the points off $C$ that must be entered from $C$ by a single extra switch.
\end{conjecture}

The insight is that the greedy climb spends exactly one switch per point it must be able to \emph{enter}, so the true invariant counts entries, not points or levels. The two matching bounds and an explicit counterexample to the naive formula (a $6$-point poset of height $3$ with $\lceil \log_2 6\rceil = 3$ yet $\mathrm{sw} = 4$) isolate the gap to a single combinatorial quantity, searchable exhaustively for $|P| \le 7$.

\begin{conjecture}[Randomised representability threshold]
For the random bounded poset on $n$ points obtained by transitively closing $G(n,p)$ on a linear order and adjoining $\bot$ and $\top$, one has $\mathrm{sw} = (1+o(1))\,n$ for constant $p$: the trivial upper bound $n-1$ is asymptotically tight for almost all bounded posets.
\end{conjecture}

Further directions: (a) determine whether the least $m$ in Theorem~\ref{thm:filtration} equals $\mathrm{sw}(P/\!\!\approx)$; (b) extend the inheritance theorem and the cluster bound to infinite clocks or infinite switch banks, where ``choose a maximal preimage'' must be replaced by a chain-completeness argument; (c) prove the phase-augmented analogue of Theorem~\ref{thm:modal}, identifying the modal theory of $\{\CW_c(n,m)\}$ with that of the finite rooted directed preorders, i.e.\ with S4.2.

Clock-and-Switch Worlds: numerical demonstrations.

This script is fully self-contained (standard library only) and illustrates,
by explicit computation on small finite orders, the results of the paper
"Clock-and-Switch Worlds: A Sharp Filtration Theorem for Finite Preorders".

A clock-and-switch world CW(n, m) is the set of pairs (clock, switches) with
clock in {0, ..., n-1} and switches a subset of {0, ..., m-1}, ordered by

    (c, S) <= (c', S')   iff   c <= c'  and  S subset of S'.

A bounded morphism f : X -> Y of preorders satisfies
    (forth)  x <= y  implies  f(x) <= f(y),
    (back)   f(x) <= q  implies  there is y >= x with f(y) = q.

Demonstrations performed below:

  1. Cardinality  |CW(n, m)| = n * 2^m  and  |CW_c(n, m)| = n * 2^m * c.
  2. The greedy climb realises every finite rooted directed poset as a
     surjective bounded morphic image of CW(1, |P| - 1).
  3. The naive greedy climb (without the "jump to the top" clause) is NOT
     monotone on the diamond -- the counterexample that motivates the clause.
  4. The two lower bounds: |P| <= n * 2^m and height(P) <= n + m - 1.
  5. Exact switch count for chains: the (l+1)-chain needs exactly l switches.
  6. Antisymmetry is inherited: the two-element cluster is unrepresentable
     (verified by exhaustive search over all maps from small worlds).
  7. Phase-augmented worlds repair this: every finite rooted directed
     preorder is an image of CW_c(1, m) with c the maximal cluster size and
     m the number of clusters -- and c cannot be lowered.
"""

from __future__ import annotations

from itertools import combinations, product
from typing import Callable, Dict, FrozenSet, List, Optional, Sequence, Set, Tuple

# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Finite preorders
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

Preorder = Tuple[Tuple[int, ...], Set[Tuple[int, int]]]
"""A finite preorder: the tuple of its elements and its <= relation as pairs."""


def transitive_reflexive_closure(
    elements: Sequence[int], edges: Sequence[Tuple[int, int]]
) -> Set[Tuple[int, int]]:
    """Reflexive-transitive closure of `edges` on `elements` (Floyd-Warshall)."""
    rel: Set[Tuple[int, int]] = {(x, x) for x in elements}
    rel |= set(edges)
    changed = True
    while changed:
        changed = False
        for a, b in list(rel):
            for c, d in list(rel):
                if b == c and (a, d) not in rel:
                    rel.add((a, d))
                    changed = True
    return rel


def make_preorder(n: int, edges: Sequence[Tuple[int, int]]) -> Preorder:
    """Build the preorder on {0,...,n-1} generated by `edges`."""
    elements = tuple(range(n))
    return elements, transitive_reflexive_closure(elements, edges)


def leq(P: Preorder) -> Callable[[int, int], bool]:
    """The order relation of `P` as a predicate."""
    _, rel = P
    return lambda x, y: (x, y) in rel


def is_rooted(P: Preorder) -> Optional[int]:
    """Return a root of `P` (a point below everything) or None."""
    elements, rel = P
    for r in elements:
        if all((r, p) in rel for p in elements):
            return r
    return None


def is_directed(P: Preorder) -> bool:
    """True iff every pair of points of `P` has a common upper bound."""
    elements, rel = P
    return all(
        any((x, z) in rel and (y, z) in rel for z in elements)
        for x in elements
        for y in elements
    )


def top_element(P: Preorder) -> Optional[int]:
    """Return a greatest element of `P` (exists when finite, nonempty, directed)."""
    elements, rel = P
    for t in elements:
        if all((p, t) in rel for p in elements):
            return t
    return None


def is_antisymmetric(P: Preorder) -> bool:
    """True iff `P` is a partial order."""
    elements, rel = P
    return all(
        not ((x, y) in rel and (y, x) in rel and x != y)
        for x in elements
        for y in elements
    )


def cluster_of(P: Preorder, p0: int) -> FrozenSet[int]:
    """The cluster of `p0`: all points mutually accessible with `p0`."""
    elements, rel = P
    return frozenset(p for p in elements if (p, p0) in rel and (p0, p) in rel)


def clusters(P: Preorder) -> List[FrozenSet[int]]:
    """The clusters of `P`, i.e. the fibres of the antisymmetrisation."""
    elements, _ = P
    seen: List[FrozenSet[int]] = []
    for p in elements:
        c = cluster_of(P, p)
        if c not in seen:
            seen.append(c)
    return seen


def height(P: Preorder) -> int:
    """The largest l with a strictly increasing chain c_0 < ... < c_l."""
    elements, rel = P

    def strict(x: int, y: int) -> bool:
        return (x, y) in rel and (y, x) not in rel

    best: Dict[int, int] = {}

    def longest_from(x: int) -> int:
        if x in best:
            return best[x]
        best[x] = 0  # guards against clusters (strict is irreflexive)
        value = 0
        for y in elements:
            if strict(x, y):
                value = max(value, 1 + longest_from(y))
        best[x] = value
        return value

    return max((longest_from(x) for x in elements), default=0)


def linear_extension(P: Preorder) -> List[int]:
    """A listing t_0, ..., t_{k-1} of a finite poset with t_i <= t_j => i <= j."""
    elements, rel = P
    remaining = list(elements)
    out: List[int] = []
    while remaining:
        for x in remaining:
            if all((y, x) not in rel or y == x or y in out for y in remaining):
                out.append(x)
                remaining.remove(x)
                break
        else:  # pragma: no cover - impossible for a finite poset
            raise ValueError("not a partial order")
    return out


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Clock-and-switch worlds
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

World = Tuple[int, FrozenSet[int]]
"""A clock-and-switch world: a clock reading and the set of switches that are on."""


def cworld(n: int, m: int) -> List[World]:
    """All n * 2^m states of CW(n, m)."""
    out: List[World] = []
    for c in range(n):
        for bits in product([False, True], repeat=m):
            out.append((c, frozenset(i for i, b in enumerate(bits) if b)))
    return out


def world_leq(w: World, v: World) -> bool:
    """Accessibility in CW(n, m): the clock advances, switches only turn on."""
    return w[0] <= v[0] and w[1] <= v[1]


def rank(w: World) -> int:
    """The rank grading: clock reading plus number of switches that are on."""
    return w[0] + len(w[1])


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Checking bounded morphisms
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

def check_bounded_morphism(
    source: Sequence[World],
    src_leq: Callable[[World, World], bool],
    P: Preorder,
    f: Callable[[World], int],
) -> Tuple[bool, bool, bool]:
    """Return (forth, back, surjective) for the candidate morphism `f`."""
    elements, _ = P
    le = leq(P)
    forth = all(le(f(x), f(y)) for x in source for y in source if src_leq(x, y))
    back = all(
        any(src_leq(x, y) and f(y) == q for y in source)
        for x in source
        for q in elements
        if le(f(x), q)
    )
    surjective = {f(x) for x in source} == set(elements)
    return forth, back, surjective


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# The greedy climb
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

def greedy_climb(P: Preorder, drop_root_switch: bool = True) -> Tuple[int, Callable[[World], int]]:
    """The greedy climb morphism from CW(1, m) onto a rooted directed poset `P`.

    Returns the number of switches m and the map itself.  With
    `drop_root_switch` the root's (no-op) switch is removed, giving m = |P| - 1.
    """
    root = is_rooted(P)
    top = top_element(P)
    if root is None or top is None:
        raise ValueError("P must be rooted and directed")
    order = linear_extension(P)
    if drop_root_switch:
        order = order[1:]  # the root always comes first, and its switch is a no-op
    le = leq(P)
    m = len(order)

    def climb(w: World) -> int:
        pos = root
        for i, target in enumerate(order):
            if i in w[1]:
                pos = target if le(pos, target) else top
        return pos

    return m, climb


def naive_climb(P: Preorder) -> Tuple[int, Callable[[World], int]]:
    """The greedy climb WITHOUT the 'jump to the top' repair clause."""
    root = is_rooted(P)
    if root is None:
        raise ValueError("P must be rooted")
    order = linear_extension(P)
    le = leq(P)

    def climb(w: World) -> int:
        pos = root
        for i, target in enumerate(order):
            if i in w[1] and le(pos, target):
                pos = target
        return pos

    return len(order), climb


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Exhaustive search for the minimal switch number
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

def exists_morphism_from_cube(P: Preorder, m: int) -> Optional[Dict[World, int]]:
    """Search for a surjective bounded morphism CW(1, m) -> P, or return None.

    Vertices of the cube are assigned in order of increasing popcount, so that
    monotonicity can be checked against already-assigned predecessors and the
    search tree pruned as early as possible.
    """
    elements, _ = P
    le = leq(P)
    worlds = sorted(cworld(1, m), key=lambda w: (len(w[1]), sorted(w[1])))
    assignment: Dict[World, int] = {}

    def predecessors(w: World) -> List[World]:
        return [v for v in assignment if world_leq(v, w)]

    def complete_ok() -> bool:
        f = assignment.__getitem__
        forth, back, surj = check_bounded_morphism(worlds, world_leq, P, f)
        return forth and back and surj

    def recurse(index: int) -> bool:
        if index == len(worlds):
            return complete_ok()
        w = worlds[index]
        preds = predecessors(w)
        for value in elements:
            if all(le(assignment[v], value) for v in preds):
                assignment[w] = value
                if recurse(index + 1):
                    return True
                del assignment[w]
        return False

    return dict(assignment) if recurse(0) else None


def switch_number(P: Preorder, max_switches: int = 6) -> Optional[int]:
    """The least m with a surjective bounded morphism CW(1, m) -> P."""
    for m in range(max_switches + 1):
        if 2 ** m < len(P[0]):
            continue  # cardinality bound
        if m < height(P):
            continue  # height bound (one clock tick)
        if exists_morphism_from_cube(P, m) is not None:
            return m
    return None


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Phase-augmented worlds
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

PWorld = Tuple[World, int]
"""A phase-augmented world: a base world together with an order-invisible phase."""


def cworld_phase(n: int, m: int, c: int) -> List[PWorld]:
    """All n * 2^m * c states of CW_c(n, m)."""
    return [(w, j) for w in cworld(n, m) for j in range(c)]


def pworld_leq(w: PWorld, v: PWorld) -> bool:
    """Accessibility in CW_c(n, m): the phase is invisible to the order."""
    return world_leq(w[0], v[0])


def phase_representation(P: Preorder) -> Tuple[int, int, Callable[[PWorld], int]]:
    """The phase-augmented representation of a finite rooted directed preorder.

    Returns (m, c, F) where m is the number of clusters, c the maximal cluster
    size, and F : CW_c(1, m) -> P a surjective bounded morphism.  The map is
    "greedy climb on the antisymmetrisation, then read the phase as a choice of
    element inside the cluster reached".
    """
    cls = clusters(P)
    c = max(len(x) for x in cls)
    reps = [min(x) for x in cls]
    index_of = {p: i for i, x in enumerate(cls) for p in x}
    le = leq(P)

    # the antisymmetrisation Q, a rooted directed poset on the clusters
    q_edges = [
        (i, j)
        for i in range(len(cls))
        for j in range(len(cls))
        if le(reps[i], reps[j])
    ]
    Q = make_preorder(len(cls), q_edges)
    m, f = greedy_climb(Q, drop_root_switch=False)

    # a fibre-surjective choice function pick(q, j)
    enumerated = [sorted(x) for x in cls]

    def pick(q: int, j: int) -> int:
        members = enumerated[q]
        return members[j] if j < len(members) else members[0]

    def F(w: PWorld) -> int:
        return pick(f(w[0]), w[1])

    return m, c, F


def check_phase_morphism(
    P: Preorder, m: int, c: int, F: Callable[[PWorld], int]
) -> Tuple[bool, bool, bool]:
    """Return (forth, back, surjective) for a candidate map out of CW_c(1, m)."""
    source = cworld_phase(1, m, c)
    elements, _ = P
    le = leq(P)
    forth = all(le(F(x), F(y)) for x in source for y in source if pworld_leq(x, y))
    back = all(
        any(pworld_leq(x, y) and F(y) == q for y in source)
        for x in source
        for q in elements
        if le(F(x), q)
    )
    surjective = {F(x) for x in source} == set(elements)
    return forth, back, surjective


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Example orders
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

def chain(k: int) -> Preorder:
    """The k-element chain 0 < 1 < ... < k-1."""
    return make_preorder(k, [(i, i + 1) for i in range(k - 1)])


def diamond() -> Preorder:
    """The diamond 0 < a, b < 1 with a = 1, b = 2 incomparable, top = 3."""
    return make_preorder(4, [(0, 1), (0, 2), (1, 3), (2, 3)])


def boolean_lattice(d: int) -> Preorder:
    """The Boolean lattice of subsets of a d-element set, as a poset on 2^d points."""
    subsets = [frozenset(s) for r in range(d + 1) for s in combinations(range(d), r)]
    index = {s: i for i, s in enumerate(subsets)}
    edges = [(index[s], index[t]) for s in subsets for t in subsets if s <= t]
    return make_preorder(len(subsets), edges)


def six_point_poset() -> Preorder:
    """A six-point bounded poset of height 3 with two incomparable mid-levels."""
    # 0 = bottom, 1 and 2 incomparable, 3 and 4 incomparable above them, 5 = top
    return make_preorder(
        6, [(0, 1), (0, 2), (1, 3), (1, 4), (2, 3), (2, 4), (3, 5), (4, 5)]
    )


def two_element_cluster() -> Preorder:
    """The two-element cluster: distinct points, each accessible from the other."""
    return make_preorder(2, [(0, 1), (1, 0)])


def clustered_preorder() -> Preorder:
    """Bottom, then a three-element cluster, then a top: clusters of sizes 1, 3, 1."""
    edges = [(0, 1), (0, 2), (0, 3), (1, 2), (2, 1), (1, 3), (3, 1), (2, 3), (3, 2)]
    edges += [(1, 4), (2, 4), (3, 4)]
    return make_preorder(5, edges)

def demo_cardinality() -> None:
    print("=" * 72)
    print("1. Cardinality of clock-and-switch worlds")
    print("=" * 72)
    for n, m in [(1, 0), (1, 3), (3, 2), (4, 4)]:
        size = len(cworld(n, m))
        print(f"  |CW({n},{m})| = {size:5d}   predicted n*2^m = {n * 2 ** m}")
        assert size == n * 2 ** m
    for n, m, c in [(1, 2, 3), (2, 3, 2)]:
        size = len(cworld_phase(n, m, c))
        print(f"  |CW_{c}({n},{m})| = {size:5d}   predicted n*2^m*c = {n * 2 ** m * c}")
        assert size == n * 2 ** m * c
    print()


def demo_greedy_climb() -> None:
    print("=" * 72)
    print("2. The greedy climb represents finite rooted directed posets")
    print("=" * 72)
    examples = [
        ("3-chain", chain(3)),
        ("5-chain", chain(5)),
        ("diamond", diamond()),
        ("Boolean lattice B_2", boolean_lattice(2)),
        ("Boolean lattice B_3", boolean_lattice(3)),
        ("6-point poset", six_point_poset()),
    ]
    for name, P in examples:
        m, f = greedy_climb(P)
        forth, back, surj = check_bounded_morphism(cworld(1, m), world_leq, P, f)
        print(
            f"  {name:22s} |P| = {len(P[0]):2d}  switches used = {m:2d}  "
            f"forth={forth}  back={back}  onto={surj}"
        )
        assert forth and back and surj
        assert m == len(P[0]) - 1
    print()


def demo_naive_climb_fails() -> None:
    print("=" * 72)
    print("3. Without 'jump to the top' the climb is not monotone (diamond)")
    print("=" * 72)
    P = diamond()
    order = linear_extension(P)
    print(f"  linear extension of the diamond: {order}")
    m, f = naive_climb(P)
    witnesses = [
        (w, v)
        for w in cworld(1, m)
        for v in cworld(1, m)
        if world_leq(w, v) and not leq(P)(f(w), f(v))
    ]
    w, v = witnesses[0]
    print(f"  switches {sorted(w[1])} climb to {f(w)}, "
          f"switches {sorted(v[1])} climb to {f(v)}")
    print(f"  but {f(w)} <= {f(v)} is {leq(P)(f(w), f(v))}: monotonicity fails.")
    m2, f2 = greedy_climb(P, drop_root_switch=False)
    forth, _, _ = check_bounded_morphism(cworld(1, m2), world_leq, P, f2)
    print(f"  with the repair clause, forth holds: {forth}")
    assert witnesses and forth
    print()


def demo_lower_bounds() -> None:
    print("=" * 72)
    print("4. The two lower bounds: cardinality and height")
    print("=" * 72)
    examples = [
        ("3-chain", chain(3)),
        ("6-chain", chain(6)),
        ("diamond", diamond()),
        ("Boolean lattice B_3", boolean_lattice(3)),
        ("6-point poset", six_point_poset()),
    ]
    print(f"  {'order':22s} {'|P|':>4s} {'height':>7s} {'log2|P|':>9s} "
          f"{'switches used':>14s}")
    for name, P in examples:
        m, f = greedy_climb(P)
        h = height(P)
        log2 = max(0, (len(P[0]) - 1).bit_length())
        print(f"  {name:22s} {len(P[0]):4d} {h:7d} {log2:9d} {m:14d}")
        # both bounds hold for the constructed representation with n = 1
        assert len(P[0]) <= 1 * 2 ** m
        assert h <= 1 + m - 1
    print()


def demo_chain_switch_count() -> None:
    print("=" * 72)
    print("5. Exact switch count for chains: the (l+1)-chain needs exactly l")
    print("=" * 72)
    for ell in range(1, 4):
        P = chain(ell + 1)
        found = switch_number(P, max_switches=ell + 1)
        print(f"  ({ell + 1})-chain: minimal number of switches = {found} "
              f"(theory: {ell})")
        assert found == ell
    print()


def demo_cluster_obstruction() -> None:
    print("=" * 72)
    print("6. Antisymmetry is inherited: the two-element cluster is unreachable")
    print("=" * 72)
    K = two_element_cluster()
    print(f"  rooted: {is_rooted(K) is not None}   directed: {is_directed(K)}   "
          f"antisymmetric: {is_antisymmetric(K)}")
    for m in range(4):
        found = exists_morphism_from_cube(K, m)
        print(f"  surjective bounded morphism from CW(1,{m}) onto the cluster: "
              f"{'YES' if found else 'none'}")
        assert found is None
    print("  (the theory says no CW(n,m) works, for any n and m)")
    print()


def demo_phase_repair() -> None:
    print("=" * 72)
    print("7. Phase-augmented worlds: the filtration lemma for preorders")
    print("=" * 72)
    examples = [
        ("two-element cluster", two_element_cluster()),
        ("bottom + 3-cluster + top", clustered_preorder()),
        ("diamond (a poset)", diamond()),
    ]
    for name, P in examples:
        sizes = sorted(len(x) for x in clusters(P))
        m, c, F = phase_representation(P)
        forth, back, surj = check_phase_morphism(P, m, c, F)
        print(f"  {name:26s} cluster sizes {sizes}  ->  CW_{c}(1,{m})  "
              f"forth={forth} back={back} onto={surj}")
        assert forth and back and surj
        assert c == max(sizes)
        assert m == len(clusters(P))
    print()
    print("  Sharpness: the number of phases can never be less than the maximal")
    print("  cluster size, since every cluster of an image of CW_c(n,m) injects")
    print("  into the c phases.  Checking the failure directly for c = 1:")
    K = two_element_cluster()
    found = any(exists_morphism_from_cube(K, m) is not None for m in range(4))
    print(f"    one phase (i.e. an ordinary world) onto the 2-cluster: "
          f"{'YES' if found else 'impossible'}")
    assert not found
    print()


def main() -> None:
    demo_cardinality()
    demo_greedy_climb()
    demo_naive_climb_fails()
    demo_lower_bounds()
    demo_chain_switch_count()
    demo_cluster_obstruction()
    demo_phase_repair()
    print("All demonstrations completed successfully.")

    main()

from __future__ import annotations

from itertools import combinations, product
from typing import Callable, Dict, FrozenSet, List, Optional, Sequence, Set, Tuple

# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Finite preorders
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

Preorder = Tuple[Tuple[int, ...], Set[Tuple[int, int]]]
"""A finite preorder: the tuple of its elements and its <= relation as pairs."""


def transitive_reflexive_closure(
    elements: Sequence[int], edges: Sequence[Tuple[int, int]]
) -> Set[Tuple[int, int]]:
    """Reflexive-transitive closure of `edges` on `elements` (Floyd-Warshall)."""
    rel: Set[Tuple[int, int]] = {(x, x) for x in elements}
    rel |= set(edges)
    changed = True
    while changed:
        changed = False
        for a, b in list(rel):
            for c, d in list(rel):
                if b == c and (a, d) not in rel:
                    rel.add((a, d))
                    changed = True
    return rel


def make_preorder(n: int, edges: Sequence[Tuple[int, int]]) -> Preorder:
    """Build the preorder on {0,...,n-1} generated by `edges`."""
    elements = tuple(range(n))
    return elements, transitive_reflexive_closure(elements, edges)


def leq(P: Preorder) -> Callable[[int, int], bool]:
    """The order relation of `P` as a predicate."""
    _, rel = P
    return lambda x, y: (x, y) in rel


def is_rooted(P: Preorder) -> Optional[int]:
    """Return a root of `P` (a point below everything) or None."""
    elements, rel = P
    for r in elements:
        if all((r, p) in rel for p in elements):
            return r
    return None


def is_directed(P: Preorder) -> bool:
    """True iff every pair of points of `P` has a common upper bound."""
    elements, rel = P
    return all(
        any((x, z) in rel and (y, z) in rel for z in elements)
        for x in elements
        for y in elements
    )


def top_element(P: Preorder) -> Optional[int]:
    """Return a greatest element of `P` (exists when finite, nonempty, directed)."""
    elements, rel = P
    for t in elements:
        if all((p, t) in rel for p in elements):
            return t
    return None


def is_antisymmetric(P: Preorder) -> bool:
    """True iff `P` is a partial order."""
    elements, rel = P
    return all(
        not ((x, y) in rel and (y, x) in rel and x != y)
        for x in elements
        for y in elements
    )


def cluster_of(P: Preorder, p0: int) -> FrozenSet[int]:
    """The cluster of `p0`: all points mutually accessible with `p0`."""
    elements, rel = P
    return frozenset(p for p in elements if (p, p0) in rel and (p0, p) in rel)


def clusters(P: Preorder) -> List[FrozenSet[int]]:
    """The clusters of `P`, i.e. the fibres of the antisymmetrisation."""
    elements, _ = P
    seen: List[FrozenSet[int]] = []
    for p in elements:
        c = cluster_of(P, p)
        if c not in seen:
            seen.append(c)
    return seen


def height(P: Preorder) -> int:
    """The largest l with a strictly increasing chain c_0 < ... < c_l."""
    elements, rel = P

    def strict(x: int, y: int) -> bool:
        return (x, y) in rel and (y, x) not in rel

    best: Dict[int, int] = {}

    def longest_from(x: int) -> int:
        if x in best:
            return best[x]
        best[x] = 0  # guards against clusters (strict is irreflexive)
        value = 0
        for y in elements:
            if strict(x, y):
                value = max(value, 1 + longest_from(y))
        best[x] = value
        return value

    return max((longest_from(x) for x in elements), default=0)


def linear_extension(P: Preorder) -> List[int]:
    """A listing t_0, ..., t_{k-1} of a finite poset with t_i <= t_j => i <= j."""
    elements, rel = P
    remaining = list(elements)
    out: List[int] = []
    while remaining:
        for x in remaining:
            if all((y, x) not in rel or y == x or y in out for y in remaining):
                out.append(x)
                remaining.remove(x)
                break
        else:  # pragma: no cover - impossible for a finite poset
            raise ValueError("not a partial order")
    return out


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Clock-and-switch worlds
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

World = Tuple[int, FrozenSet[int]]
"""A clock-and-switch world: a clock reading and the set of switches that are on."""


def cworld(n: int, m: int) -> List[World]:
    """All n * 2^m states of CW(n, m)."""
    out: List[World] = []
    for c in range(n):
        for bits in product([False, True], repeat=m):
            out.append((c, frozenset(i for i, b in enumerate(bits) if b)))
    return out


def world_leq(w: World, v: World) -> bool:
    """Accessibility in CW(n, m): the clock advances, switches only turn on."""
    return w[0] <= v[0] and w[1] <= v[1]


def rank(w: World) -> int:
    """The rank grading: clock reading plus number of switches that are on."""
    return w[0] + len(w[1])


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Checking bounded morphisms
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

def check_bounded_morphism(
    source: Sequence[World],
    src_leq: Callable[[World, World], bool],
    P: Preorder,
    f: Callable[[World], int],
) -> Tuple[bool, bool, bool]:
    """Return (forth, back, surjective) for the candidate morphism `f`."""
    elements, _ = P
    le = leq(P)
    forth = all(le(f(x), f(y)) for x in source for y in source if src_leq(x, y))
    back = all(
        any(src_leq(x, y) and f(y) == q for y in source)
        for x in source
        for q in elements
        if le(f(x), q)
    )
    surjective = {f(x) for x in source} == set(elements)
    return forth, back, surjective


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# The greedy climb
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

def greedy_climb(P: Preorder, drop_root_switch: bool = True) -> Tuple[int, Callable[[World], int]]:
    """The greedy climb morphism from CW(1, m) onto a rooted directed poset `P`.

    Returns the number of switches m and the map itself.  With
    `drop_root_switch` the root's (no-op) switch is removed, giving m = |P| - 1.
    """
    root = is_rooted(P)
    top = top_element(P)
    if root is None or top is None:
        raise ValueError("P must be rooted and directed")
    order = linear_extension(P)
    if drop_root_switch:
        order = order[1:]  # the root always comes first, and its switch is a no-op
    le = leq(P)
    m = len(order)

    def climb(w: World) -> int:
        pos = root
        for i, target in enumerate(order):
            if i in w[1]:
                pos = target if le(pos, target) else top
        return pos

    return m, climb


def naive_climb(P: Preorder) -> Tuple[int, Callable[[World], int]]:
    """The greedy climb WITHOUT the 'jump to the top' repair clause."""
    root = is_rooted(P)
    if root is None:
        raise ValueError("P must be rooted")
    order = linear_extension(P)
    le = leq(P)

    def climb(w: World) -> int:
        pos = root
        for i, target in enumerate(order):
            if i in w[1] and le(pos, target):
                pos = target
        return pos

    return len(order), climb


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Exhaustive search for the minimal switch number
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

def exists_morphism_from_cube(P: Preorder, m: int) -> Optional[Dict[World, int]]:
    """Search for a surjective bounded morphism CW(1, m) -> P, or return None.

    Vertices of the cube are assigned in order of increasing popcount, so that
    monotonicity can be checked against already-assigned predecessors and the
    search tree pruned as early as possible.
    """
    elements, _ = P
    le = leq(P)
    worlds = sorted(cworld(1, m), key=lambda w: (len(w[1]), sorted(w[1])))
    assignment: Dict[World, int] = {}

    def predecessors(w: World) -> List[World]:
        return [v for v in assignment if world_leq(v, w)]

    def complete_ok() -> bool:
        f = assignment.__getitem__
        forth, back, surj = check_bounded_morphism(worlds, world_leq, P, f)
        return forth and back and surj

    def recurse(index: int) -> bool:
        if index == len(worlds):
            return complete_ok()
        w = worlds[index]
        preds = predecessors(w)
        for value in elements:
            if all(le(assignment[v], value) for v in preds):
                assignment[w] = value
                if recurse(index + 1):
                    return True
                del assignment[w]
        return False

    return dict(assignment) if recurse(0) else None


def switch_number(P: Preorder, max_switches: int = 6) -> Optional[int]:
    """The least m with a surjective bounded morphism CW(1, m) -> P."""
    for m in range(max_switches + 1):
        if 2 ** m < len(P[0]):
            continue  # cardinality bound
        if m < height(P):
            continue  # height bound (one clock tick)
        if exists_morphism_from_cube(P, m) is not None:
            return m
    return None


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Phase-augmented worlds
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

PWorld = Tuple[World, int]
"""A phase-augmented world: a base world together with an order-invisible phase."""


def cworld_phase(n: int, m: int, c: int) -> List[PWorld]:
    """All n * 2^m * c states of CW_c(n, m)."""
    return [(w, j) for w in cworld(n, m) for j in range(c)]


def pworld_leq(w: PWorld, v: PWorld) -> bool:
    """Accessibility in CW_c(n, m): the phase is invisible to the order."""
    return world_leq(w[0], v[0])


def phase_representation(P: Preorder) -> Tuple[int, int, Callable[[PWorld], int]]:
    """The phase-augmented representation of a finite rooted directed preorder.

    Returns (m, c, F) where m is the number of clusters, c the maximal cluster
    size, and F : CW_c(1, m) -> P a surjective bounded morphism.  The map is
    "greedy climb on the antisymmetrisation, then read the phase as a choice of
    element inside the cluster reached".
    """
    cls = clusters(P)
    c = max(len(x) for x in cls)
    reps = [min(x) for x in cls]
    index_of = {p: i for i, x in enumerate(cls) for p in x}
    le = leq(P)

    # the antisymmetrisation Q, a rooted directed poset on the clusters
    q_edges = [
        (i, j)
        for i in range(len(cls))
        for j in range(len(cls))
        if le(reps[i], reps[j])
    ]
    Q = make_preorder(len(cls), q_edges)
    m, f = greedy_climb(Q, drop_root_switch=False)

    # a fibre-surjective choice function pick(q, j)
    enumerated = [sorted(x) for x in cls]

    def pick(q: int, j: int) -> int:
        members = enumerated[q]
        return members[j] if j < len(members) else members[0]

    def F(w: PWorld) -> int:
        return pick(f(w[0]), w[1])

    return m, c, F


def check_phase_morphism(
    P: Preorder, m: int, c: int, F: Callable[[PWorld], int]
) -> Tuple[bool, bool, bool]:
    """Return (forth, back, surjective) for a candidate map out of CW_c(1, m)."""
    source = cworld_phase(1, m, c)
    elements, _ = P
    le = leq(P)
    forth = all(le(F(x), F(y)) for x in source for y in source if pworld_leq(x, y))
    back = all(
        any(pworld_leq(x, y) and F(y) == q for y in source)
        for x in source
        for q in elements
        if le(F(x), q)
    )
    surjective = {F(x) for x in source} == set(elements)
    return forth, back, surjective

# Example orders
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

def chain(k: int) -> Preorder:
    """The k-element chain 0 < 1 < ... < k-1."""
    return make_preorder(k, [(i, i + 1) for i in range(k - 1)])


def diamond() -> Preorder:
    """The diamond 0 < a, b < 1 with a = 1, b = 2 incomparable, top = 3."""
    return make_preorder(4, [(0, 1), (0, 2), (1, 3), (2, 3)])


def boolean_lattice(d: int) -> Preorder:
    """The Boolean lattice of subsets of a d-element set, as a poset on 2^d points."""
    subsets = [frozenset(s) for r in range(d + 1) for s in combinations(range(d), r)]
    index = {s: i for i, s in enumerate(subsets)}
    edges = [(index[s], index[t]) for s in subsets for t in subsets if s <= t]
    return make_preorder(len(subsets), edges)


def six_point_poset() -> Preorder:
    """A six-point bounded poset of height 3 with two incomparable mid-levels."""
    # 0 = bottom, 1 and 2 incomparable, 3 and 4 incomparable above them, 5 = top
    return make_preorder(
        6, [(0, 1), (0, 2), (1, 3), (1, 4), (2, 3), (2, 4), (3, 5), (4, 5)]
    )


def two_element_cluster() -> Preorder:
    """The two-element cluster: distinct points, each accessible from the other."""
    return make_preorder(2, [(0, 1), (1, 0)])


def clustered_preorder() -> Preorder:
    """Bottom, then a three-element cluster, then a top: clusters of sizes 1, 3, 1."""
    edges = [(0, 1), (0, 2), (0, 3), (1, 2), (2, 1), (1, 3), (3, 1), (2, 3), (3, 2)]
    edges += [(1, 4), (2, 4), (3, 4)]
    return make_preorder(5, edges)

def closure(n: int, edges: Sequence[Tuple[int, int]]) -> Set[Tuple[int, int]]:
    """Reflexive-transitive closure of `edges` on {0, ..., n-1}."""
    rel: Set[Tuple[int, int]] = {(x, x) for x in range(n)} | set(edges)
    changed = True
    while changed:
        changed = False
        for a, b in list(rel):
            for c, d in list(rel):
                if b == c and (a, d) not in rel:
                    rel.add((a, d))
                    changed = True
    return rel


def stack_of_clusters(sizes: Sequence[int]) -> Tuple[int, Set[Tuple[int, int]], List[List[int]]]:
    """The preorder whose clusters of the given sizes are stacked in a chain."""
    groups: List[List[int]] = []
    next_id = 0
    for s in sizes:
        groups.append(list(range(next_id, next_id + s)))
        next_id += s
    edges: List[Tuple[int, int]] = []
    for q, g in enumerate(groups):
        for p in g:
            for p2 in g:
                edges.append((p, p2))
        if q + 1 < len(groups):
            for p in g:
                for p2 in groups[q + 1]:
                    edges.append((p, p2))
    return next_id, closure(next_id, edges), groups


def cube(m: int) -> List[World]:
    """The states of the one-tick clock-and-switch world CW(1, m)."""
    return [(0, frozenset(i for i, b in enumerate(bits) if b))
            for bits in product([False, True], repeat=m)]


def world_leq(w: World, v: World) -> bool:
    """Accessibility in CW(1, m)."""
    return w[0] <= v[0] and w[1] <= v[1]


def greedy_climb_on_chain(m: int) -> Callable[[World], int]:
    """Greedy climb onto the m-element chain of clusters (identity linear extension)."""
    def climb(w: World) -> int:
        pos = 0
        for i in range(m):
            if i in w[1]:
                pos = i if pos <= i else m - 1
        return pos
    return climb


def phase_map(groups: List[List[int]], c: int) -> Callable[[PWorld], int]:
    """F(w, j) = pick(climb(w), j) with pick a choice of element inside a cluster."""
    m = len(groups)
    climb = greedy_climb_on_chain(m)

    def pick(q: int, j: int) -> int:
        members = groups[q]
        return members[j] if j < len(members) else members[0]

    return lambda state: pick(climb(state[0]), state[1])

        for x in states for q in range(n) if le(F(x), q)
    )
    onto = {F(x) for x in states} == set(range(n))
    return forth, back, onto

from __future__ import annotations

from typing import Callable, FrozenSet, List, Optional, Sequence, Set, Tuple

World = Tuple[int, FrozenSet[int]]


def closure(n: int, edges: Sequence[Tuple[int, int]]) -> Set[Tuple[int, int]]:
    """Reflexive-transitive closure of `edges` on {0, ..., n-1}."""
    rel: Set[Tuple[int, int]] = {(x, x) for x in range(n)} | set(edges)
    changed = True
    while changed:
        changed = False
        for a, b in list(rel):
            for cc, d in list(rel):
                if b == cc and (a, d) not in rel:
                    rel.add((a, d))
                    changed = True
    return rel


def linear_extension(n: int, rel: Set[Tuple[int, int]]) -> List[int]:
    """A listing t_0, ..., t_{n-1} with t_i <= t_j implying i <= j (topological sort)."""
    remaining, out = list(range(n)), []
    while remaining:
        for x in remaining:
            if all((y, x) not in rel or y == x or y in out for y in remaining):
                out.append(x)
                remaining.remove(x)
                break
        else:  # pragma: no cover
            raise ValueError("input is not a partial order")
    return out


def greedy_climb(
    n: int, edges: Sequence[Tuple[int, int]]
) -> Tuple[int, Callable[[World], int]]:
    """Build the greedy climb morphism CW(1, n-1) -> P.

    `P` is the poset on {0, ..., n-1} generated by `edges`; it must be rooted and
    directed.  Returns the number of switches and the morphism itself.
    """
    rel = closure(n, edges)
    root: Optional[int] = next((r for r in range(n) if all((r, p) in rel for p in range(n))), None)
    top: Optional[int] = next((t for t in range(n) if all((p, t) in rel for p in range(n))), None)
    if root is None or top is None:
        raise ValueError("the poset must be rooted and directed")

    order = linear_extension(n, rel)[1:]     # the root's switch is a no-op: drop it

    def climb(w: World) -> int:
        pos = root
        for i, target in enumerate(order):
            if i in w[1]:
                pos = target if (pos, target) in rel else top
        return pos

    return len(order), climb

from __future__ import annotations

from itertools import product
from math import ceil, log2
from typing import Callable, Dict, FrozenSet, List, Optional, Sequence, Set, Tuple

World = Tuple[int, FrozenSet[int]]


def cube(m: int) -> List[World]:
    """The states of the one-tick world CW(1, m), ordered by increasing popcount."""
    out = [(0, frozenset(i for i, b in enumerate(bits) if b))
           for bits in product([False, True], repeat=m)]
    return sorted(out, key=lambda w: (len(w[1]), sorted(w[1])))


def world_leq(w: World, v: World) -> bool:
    """Accessibility: the clock advances and switches only turn on."""
    return w[0] <= v[0] and w[1] <= v[1]


def strict_height(n: int, rel: Set[Tuple[int, int]]) -> int:
    """Length of the longest strictly increasing chain."""
    memo: Dict[int, int] = {}

    def longest(x: int) -> int:
        if x in memo:
            return memo[x]
        memo[x] = 0
        memo[x] = max((1 + longest(y) for y in range(n)
                       if (x, y) in rel and (y, x) not in rel), default=0)
        return memo[x]

    return max((longest(x) for x in range(n)), default=0)


def is_bounded_morphism(
    worlds: Sequence[World], n: int, rel: Set[Tuple[int, int]], f: Dict[World, int]
) -> bool:
    """Check forth, back and surjectivity of the tabulated map `f`."""
    forth = all((f[x], f[y]) in rel for x in worlds for y in worlds if world_leq(x, y))
    if not forth:
        return False
    back = all(
        any(world_leq(x, y) and f[y] == q for y in worlds)
        for x in worlds for q in range(n) if (f[x], q) in rel
    )
    return back and {f[x] for x in worlds} == set(range(n))


def switch_number(n: int, rel: Set[Tuple[int, int]], max_switches: int = 6) -> Optional[int]:
    """Least m admitting a surjective bounded morphism CW(1, m) -> P, or None.

    The search assigns values to cube vertices in order of increasing popcount and
    prunes the moment monotonicity fails against an already-assigned predecessor.
    Outer-loop pruning uses the cardinality bound 2^m >= |P| and, for one clock tick,
    the height bound m >= height(P).
    """
    lower = max(ceil(log2(n)) if n > 1 else 0, strict_height(n, rel))
    for m in range(lower, max_switches + 1):
        worlds = cube(m)
        assignment: Dict[World, int] = {}

        def recurse(index: int) -> bool:
            if index == len(worlds):
                return is_bounded_morphism(worlds, n, rel, assignment)
            w = worlds[index]
            preds = [v for v in assignment if world_leq(v, w)]
            for value in range(n):
                if all((assignment[v], value) in rel for v in preds):
                    assignment[w] = value
                    if recurse(index + 1):
                        return True
                    del assignment[w]
            return False

        if recurse(0):
            return m
    return None

from __future__ import annotations

from typing import Callable, Dict, FrozenSet, List, Sequence, Set, Tuple

World = Tuple[int, FrozenSet[int]]
PWorld = Tuple[World, int]


def closure(n: int, edges: Sequence[Tuple[int, int]]) -> Set[Tuple[int, int]]:
    """Reflexive-transitive closure of `edges` on {0, ..., n-1}."""
    rel: Set[Tuple[int, int]] = {(x, x) for x in range(n)} | set(edges)
    changed = True
    while changed:
        changed = False
        for a, b in list(rel):
            for c, d in list(rel):
                if b == c and (a, d) not in rel:
                    rel.add((a, d))
                    changed = True
    return rel


def clusters(n: int, rel: Set[Tuple[int, int]]) -> List[List[int]]:
    """The clusters of the preorder: the classes of mutual accessibility."""
    seen: List[FrozenSet[int]] = []
    for p in range(n):
        cl = frozenset(q for q in range(n) if (p, q) in rel and (q, p) in rel)
        if cl not in seen:
            seen.append(cl)
    return [sorted(cl) for cl in seen]


def greedy_climb_on(k: int, rel: Set[Tuple[int, int]]) -> Tuple[int, Callable[[World], int]]:
    """Greedy climb morphism CW(1, k) -> Q for a rooted directed poset Q on k points."""
    root = next(r for r in range(k) if all((r, p) in rel for p in range(k)))
    top = next(t for t in range(k) if all((p, t) in rel for p in range(k)))
    remaining, order = list(range(k)), []
    while remaining:
        for x in remaining:
            if all((y, x) not in rel or y == x or y in order for y in remaining):
                order.append(x)
                remaining.remove(x)
                break

    def climb(w: World) -> int:
        pos = root
        for i, target in enumerate(order):
            if i in w[1]:
                pos = target if (pos, target) in rel else top
        return pos

    return k, climb


def phase_representation(
    n: int, edges: Sequence[Tuple[int, int]]
) -> Tuple[int, int, Callable[[PWorld], int]]:
    """Represent a finite rooted directed preorder by a phase-augmented world.

    Returns (m, c, F) with m the number of clusters, c the largest cluster size, and
    F : CW_c(1, m) -> P a surjective bounded morphism.  The map is
    "greedy climb on the antisymmetrisation, then read the phase as a choice of
    element inside the cluster reached".
    """
    rel = closure(n, edges)
    cls = clusters(n, rel)
    m, c = len(cls), max(len(cl) for cl in cls)
    reps = [cl[0] for cl in cls]

    q_edges = [(i, j) for i in range(m) for j in range(m) if (reps[i], reps[j]) in rel]
    q_rel = closure(m, q_edges)
    _, f = greedy_climb_on(m, q_rel)

    def pick(q: int, j: int) -> int:
        members = cls[q]
        return members[j] if j < len(members) else members[0]

    def F(state: PWorld) -> int:
        return pick(f(state[0]), state[1])

    return m, c, F

  "interactive_layout": "# Clocks, Switches, and the Shape of Possibility

### A guided tour of the filtration theorem for finite ordered sets

---

## 1. A machine with two kinds of memory

Picture the simplest irreversible machine you can. It has a **clock** that ticks forward through $n$ positions and never back, and a bank of $m$ **switches**, each of which starts off and, once flipped on, stays on forever. A *state* is a clock reading together with the set of switches currently on. One state **leads to** another exactly when the clock has not gone backwards and no switch has been un-flipped.

Write $\mathrm{CW}(n,m)$ for this ordered set of states. Geometrically it is a product: a line of $n$ points crossed with an $m$-dimensional cube, so
$$|\mathrm{CW}(n,m)| = n \cdot 2^m .$$

It is the canonical model of *monotone resource accumulation* — time that only advances, commitments that only pile up. The question of this page is:

> **Which finite state spaces are faithful shadows of such a machine?**

The answer is three words long, and getting it required discovering an obstruction nobody ordered and then buying exactly enough new structure to pay it off.

---

## 2. What "faithful shadow" must mean

A merely order-preserving surjection is worthless: crush everything to one point and you have "represented" a point by any machine at all. We need a map that also creates no illusions about what is *not* possible.

A map $f : X \to Y$ between ordered sets is a **bounded morphism** when:

- **Forth.** $x \le y \Rightarrow f(x) \le f(y)$ — every transition upstairs is visible downstairs.
- **Back.** $f(x) \le q \Rightarrow$ there is $y \ge x$ with $f(y) = q$ — every transition downstairs can be *lifted*: whatever the shadow can do next, the machine really can do.

<details>
<summary><strong>Why the back condition is the one that matters</strong> (click to expand)</summary>

Forth alone lets the map forget structure freely. Back says the map is *locally exact*: standing at $x$, the set of possibilities you see from $f(x)$ in the shadow is precisely the $f$-image of the possibilities the machine actually has from $x$.

This is not an aesthetic preference. Bounded morphisms are exactly the maps along which [modal logic](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/logic-modal/) is invariant: if $f : X \twoheadrightarrow Y$ is a surjective bounded morphism, then $X$ and $Y$ validate exactly the same modal formulas. So "faithful shadow" is forced on us by the logic of possibility itself. The same notion appears in the literature under the names *p-morphism* and *bounded morphism*, and in the theory of [Kripke frames](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kripke_semantics) it is the standard structure-preserving map.
</details>

Call a finite ordered set $P$ **representable** if there is a surjective bounded morphism $\mathrm{CW}(n,m) \twoheadrightarrow P$ for some $n, m$.

Two representations are immediate. **Forget the switches**, $w \mapsto \mathrm{clock}(w)$, maps onto the $n$-chain. **Count the switches that are on**, $w \mapsto \#\{b : \mathrm{switch}_b(w) = \mathrm{on}\}$, maps the $m$-cube onto the chain with $m+1$ points. Both satisfy Back for the obvious reason: to go higher, flip more switches.

---

## 3. The greedy climb — play with it

Here is the construction that answers the question in the positive direction. Let $P$ be a finite ordered set that is **rooted** (a point $r$ below everything) and **directed** (any two points have a common upper bound — for finite $P$, equivalently a top $\top$). Take a **linear extension** $t_0, t_1, \dots, t_{k-1}$: a listing of all points in which $t_i \le t_j$ forces $i \le j$. Attach one switch to each point, and walk:

> Start at $r$. Read the switches left to right. When switch $i$ is on: **jump to $t_i$** if you are still below $t_i$; otherwise **jump to the top $\top$**. When switch $i$ is off, stand still.

The widget below runs this walk on all $2^m$ switch configurations at once. The cube on the right is the machine, laid out in columns by how many switches are on; each vertex is coloured by the point of $P$ it climbs to. Hover a vertex to see the trace. Then **switch off the repair clause** and watch red edges — monotonicity violations — appear.

{{interactive_demo:0}}

**Things to try.**
1. Pick the **diamond** and turn the repair clause off. Configuration $\{b\}$ climbs to $b$; the *larger* configuration $\{a,b\}$ climbs to $a$; and $b \not\le a$. Turning on more switches moved you *down*. This is the exact failure the "jump to the top" clause repairs.
2. Press **next linear extension** repeatedly. The map changes completely, but forth, back and onto all keep holding — the theorem does not depend on which extension you chose.
3. Notice that the switch attached to the root is always a no-op: you start at the root, so jumping there changes nothing. That is why $|P| - 1$ switches always suffice.

<details>
<summary><strong>The proof, in three paragraphs</strong></summary>

**Forth.** By induction on the number of steps. Suppose the climbs of $s$ and of the larger configuration $s'$ satisfy $W_s(i) \le W_{s'}(i)$. If $s_i$ is off, the left side stands still and the right side never descends. If $s_i$ is on then so is $s'_i$; either $W_{s'}(i) \le t_i$, in which case $W_s(i) \le t_i$ too and both jump to $t_i$, or $W_{s'}(i) \not\le t_i$ and the right side jumps to $\top$, which dominates everything. The repair clause is *used precisely here*.

**Back.** Given $\Phi(w) \le t_j$, turn on switch $j$ in addition to the ones already on. Because $t$ is a linear extension, every point below $t_j$ occurs at an index $\le j$, so when the climb arrives at index $j$ it is still below $t_j$; the "$\le t_i$" branch fires and the climb lands exactly on $t_j$, and no later switch is on to move it away. The resulting world is above $w$, as Back requires.

**Onto.** Apply Back at the all-off world, whose image is the root $r$, which is below every $t_j$.
</details>

**Theorem (Representation).** *Every finite rooted directed partial order is a surjective bounded morphic image of $\mathrm{CW}(1, |P| - 1)$, via the greedy climb along any linear extension.*
